title: White Frog Turns Chaos, Cynicism, and the Paranormal Into Punk on 'Don't Let the Bastards Grind You Down'
excerpt: On Don’t Let the Bastards Grind You Down, Richard Harris and Liam Guest build an eccentric world where social frustration, antihistamines, haunted houses, open mic weirdos, generational identity, missing explorers, and the occasional swarm of flies somehow belong on the same record. It shouldn’t work nearly as well as it does.
content:
West Midlands punk duo White Frog have little interest in making punk predictable. On Don’t Let the Bastards Grind You Down, Richard Harris and Liam Guest build an eccentric world where social frustration, antihistamines, haunted houses, open mic weirdos, generational identity, missing explorers, and the occasional swarm of flies somehow belong on the same record. It shouldn’t work nearly as well as it does.

The album opens by immediately establishing White Frog’s surrealist streak, imagining the arrival of “frog people” alongside the possibility of a society stripped of greed, suffering, and inequality. It’s absurd on the surface, but that tension between comedy and sincerity becomes one of the album’s strongest qualities. White Frog can make a joke without making the subject meaningless.

That philosophy runs throughout the record. “The Pollen's Evil” turns hay fever into punk antagonism, while “I Want the Drugs” takes the equally mundane act of reaching for antihistamines and exaggerates it into something considerably more dramatic. “Flies” is, quite literally, about flies. White Frog understands that punk doesn’t always need a grand political crisis to justify its existence. Sometimes irritation is enough.

Elsewhere, reality becomes stranger than fiction. The title track draws from a speeding court case, while “Grave in Your Garden” heads toward paranormal territory through the story of a haunted house in rural Flintshire, North Wales. The latter has become one of the project’s standouts, surpassing 20,000 YouTube views, while “Flies” has reached more than 10,000.

The album becomes more character-driven with “Wendy,” “Laura,” and “All My Friends Are Weirdos,” drawing inspiration from real people and the environments around the band. “Gen X Millennial” examines the cultural grey area between generations, while “Lockdown Days” revisits an era most people would probably rather forget. Then there’s “The Ballad of Michael Rockefeller,” which takes the American explorer's disappearance into darker historical territory.

White Frog’s influences, from the Sex Pistols to The Mighty Boosh, make increasingly more sense as the record unfolds. There’s punk abrasion here, but also distinctly British absurdism and spoken-word observation reminiscent of artists like Sleaford Mods and The Streets.

Beneath all the sarcasm, paranormal fascination, and everyday chaos, however, White Frog leaves something unexpectedly sincere behind. Don’t Let the Bastards Grind You Down is ultimately about how strange life can get, how badly people can handle it, and the possibility that we might still choose to be better anyway.

Your album moves between ridiculous everyday frustrations, real-life experiences, social commentary, and genuinely dark subject matter. How do you decide when an idea is funny enough, strange enough, or important enough to become a White Frog song?

It's spontaneous and often occurs at the weirdest of times, usually when im going about my everyday business, but it often happens when thoughts and memories are triggered

“Grave in Your Garden” takes the record deep into paranormal territory. What is the real story behind the haunted house in Flintshire, and how much of that experience made its way directly into the song?

Before Liam and I were a band, we were paranormal investigators, so we both have an interest in the paranormal. We traveled to that village in North Wales to shoot the video, and I have to say what a lovely place it was. The entire story is explained in the song, and if you need more clarity, watch an episode called The Monk on BBC iPlayer, presented by Sian Eleri 

There’s an interesting contrast between the chaos of White Frog’s music and the surprisingly optimistic moral underneath the album. Was that message intentional from the beginning, or did you recognize it once the record came together?

White Frog has always been fun, tongue-in-cheek, dark humor, and the paranormal; it just fits our persona, but there will always be morals because I like happy endings

Songs like “Wendy,” “Laura,” and “All My Friends Are Weirdos” pull directly from people and spaces around you. How important is documenting your immediate community and its characters to White Frog’s identity?

We write about the world that is happening in front of us, and yes, I have had some unfortunate experiences, but I have also met some amazing people. The world is an amazing and diverse place; every moment has an opportunity to cherish 

From the Sex Pistols to The Mighty Boosh, your influences cross punk, comedy, surrealism, and British culture. What did each of you bring into White Frog that helped turn those seemingly unrelated influences into one world?

Conversations with Liam trigger thoughts, points of view, and memories that fit into what we do. Liam has also written songs himself, one of which made the last release. We were asked about our inspirations, and so the sex pistols and the Mighty Boosh were the closest thing I could think of to what we do, as we were both inspired by them, but we often get compared to Sleaford Mods and The Streets, which I will take, but that wasn't what we were going for.
